speaker_role: independent educational consultant/counseling office (College Calm, referring to 'our office' and 'our students')
commercial_incentive: yes - references the consultancy's own students and other in-house videos
key_insights: Demonstrated interest matters most to smaller private colleges concerned about yield (the share of admits who enroll), and much less to large public systems like the UCs or University of Wisconsin
Every college's Common Data Set discloses whether they treat 'level of applicant's interest' as very important, important, considered, or not considered, and students should check this per school
Applying early decision is described as the strongest possible demonstrated-interest signal since it removes yield uncertainty entirely for the college
Restrictive early action still shows commitment because the student forgoes applying early to any other private school
Thoughtfully completing optional supplemental essay questions is itself a demonstrated-interest signal, since it shows extra effort beyond the required minimum

Highly selective 'name brand' schools (e.g., Harvard) often don't weigh demonstrated interest heavily since so many applicants are already highly interested, so time is better spent on 'target' schools where it matters more
Colleges reportedly track email engagement (opens/clicks) via customer-service software, though the speaker says this is not usually a deciding factor by itself
specific_numbers_or_facts: Cited example: American University's Common Data Set lists secondary school rigor and academic GPA as 'very important' and level of applicant interest also as an important factor, per the speaker's review of that document
notable_or_distinctive: Walks through the Common Data Set as a concrete, checkable public source for determining exactly how much a specific college weighs demonstrated interest, rather than relying on guesswork.
reliability_notes: Solid grounding in the Common Data Set as a real public document, but claims about email tracking and specific college practices are generalized and not sourced to a specific institution beyond the American University example; video is about 7 years old and school policies may have since changed.
